articles.text: When I was five years old, one of the largest hurricanes on record in the Atlantic Ocean, Superstorm Sandy, took the lives of 233 people from the Caribbean to Canada in October of 2012. Since then, over 16 hurricanes (also known as tropical cyclones) have taken the lives and homes of thousands in the United States. I remember the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy when the sidewalk turned to a shore when waves of knee-deep water crashed at my doorstep. I remember the hanging light in the basement which brushed across the water as it swung, and a power outage that lasted weeks. And now, 10 years later, as a sophomore at Piedmont High School, I ask where my mom’s wedding dress or where our childhood photos went. My parents respond: Lost to the flood waters, weren’t they? I am grateful that we were so lucky to remain safe and healthy during the hurricane compared to the thousands of victims who faced personal and financial crises in the aftermath. But I am left to worry in recent days when new hurricanes and disasters occur everywhere in our world, including in the United States as Hurricane Ian has already claimed the lives of more than 80 people. It is difficult for many to imagine the immense loss and pain that millions across the world are facing due to extreme weather conditions fueled by climate change. We have control over our lives and decisions. We must acknowledge our privileges and use them to the advantage of the world. This does not always mean immense strides and doesn’t mean billions of dollars. It means evaluating decisions in our everyday life. When you ask yourself if you are doing what you can to lessen the destruction. Doing your part can include remaining informed, spreading awareness, supporting environmental campaigns, and being aware of your actions and decisions. I am a member of Piedmont High’s Green Club, which is working to do our part. I understand that there are far too many people in the world who are suffering devastations worth a thousand lifetimes, people who no longer have stable access to electricity, and whose childhood homes are turning to ruin under salt water. As a high school student and a member of the next generation I want your attention. I seek understanding and urgency. We, the youth, need your eyes and your humanity for the good of our future, for the lives of billions, and for justice to families who have lost so much. We can no longer bear to read the news every day and hear of disasters that read like a literary tragedy. We can no longer bear the collective burden that grows due to simple habits that have become our liabilities. A first and meaningful step is for residents to join the Piedmont Climate Challenge at piedmontclimatechallange.org. I encourage you to take part in this movement to save not only the earth, but those who walk beside us and who tread closely behind. In the months ahead, I intend to share ways you can contribute to and support our community and beyond to address climate change – the greatest challenge of our generation. Clea Villaluz is a sophomore at Piedmont High School and a member of the school’s Green Club. She plans to write a monthly column on environmental topics. “Is it good management, or are you just having a run of good luck?”
articles.title: Hurricane Ian part of a continuing pattern

articles.text: As a long-time Piedmont resident with extensive development experience, I urge the City Council not to vote on the proposed rezoning plan until after the next election. Serious issues have been raised concerning the plan. These demand more review and community input. This is particularly true concerning planned major construction of 16 new units of housing in the center of town near Havens school, and over 100 units of new housing on a very congested Moraga Ave. The most important issue we can all agree on is that any plan must ensure the safety of our children and all residents. We can also agree that current traffic in the center of Piedmont near Havens school is currently congested and often dangerous at the beginning and end of school days. We can also agree that Moraga Ave. is very congested right now during peak hours. The proposed 16 units of housing, along with the major construction to build the units, poses significant future safety issues for our children. Given the extensive use of Coaches field for youth activities, a proposal for 100+ units of housing in a very congested area poses clear safety issues. In spite of these clear risks, it is my understanding that the City has not had a traffic engineer or safety specialist formally study these plans. The City Administrator recently basically said not to worry; this is just a plan, and any future development can be debated by the City Council. No big deal. But any developer or expert knows this is simply wrong. Once the plan is submitted to the state, it takes on a life of its own based on current state laws. Future City Councils will not be able to block it. We must make sure the plan is sound now. What is the rush to judgement? We have an election coming up. Let the new City Council review the plan and make the final decision on the plan. Finally, the City Charter clearly states that all residents should vote on zoning changes. The City Council and Administrator seem to think they can ignore that and that they know best. What are they afraid of? Let the residents vote on a clearly laid out plan supported by traffic and safety experts. Let’s do this right. Our children deserve it.
articles.title: Let residents vote on housing plan

articles.text: Join Fire Chief Brannigan for citywide drill on November 5 Many Piedmonters vividly remember the 1991 Tunnel Fire in the Oakland hills, which killed 25 people and destroyed more than 2,500 homes. While Piedmont escaped the devastation 26 years ago, the threat remains today, even more present now because of climate change, which has made wildfires more frequent and destructive. As your Fire Chief, I strive daily to ensure our City government is poised to protect this community in a disaster. But I also know that in an emergency, the best efforts of public agencies alone will not be enough. Our community needs to prepare, too. Today, I ask every Piedmonter to take three simple steps to be more ready for a wildfire. 1. First, make sure we can reach you in a disaster. If you aren’t yet registered for AC Alert emergency notifications, sign up now. Piedmont and Alameda County public safety officials will use AC Alert to send evacuation warnings and orders in a fire, earthquake, or other emergency. Visit acalert.org or text your zip code to 888-777 now to register. I also encourage everyone to bookmark community.zonehaven.com on your computer and phone. In a wildfire, emergency responders will use this site to post real-time, location-specific evacuation instructions and updates. 2. The next thing everyone should do is pack or refresh a “go-bag.” In a wildfire, you could have only moments to leave. Everyone in your household should have a go-bag ready with the items they’ll need if they had to evacuate, like a map, cash, and a paper list of phone numbers for essential contacts. Make sure your go-bag is light enough to carry in case you need to leave your vehicle and evacuate on foot – a real possibility in a disaster. 3. Finally, think about what routes you would use to evacuate in a fire. Identify two routes away from your home by car and two by foot. Mark them on the map you keep in your go-bag. For driving routes, focus on main roads that connect with major streets and highways. Bigger roads with more capacity are less likely to get blocked during an evacuation. I encourage everyone to review and practice your evacuation routes with your household, carrying your go-bags with you. Regular practice ensures everyone will know what to do in an emergency, when you must act quickly. Wildfire Evacuation Drill in Piedmont The City of Piedmont will hold its first-ever wildfire evacuation drill on Saturday, November 5. Residents in the Maxwelton neighborhood above Moraga will practice evacuating their homes, while the rest of the City is invited to participate with an at-home preparedness activity. Afterwards, come to the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, at 10 a.m. for a debriefing where you’ll have the opportunity to share observations from your experience, ask questions, and speak directly with emergency responders. I invite everyone to visit piedmont.ca.gov/wildfiredrill to learn more and sign up to participate. Share this link with your friends, family, and neighbors. The more we all take steps to prepare, the stronger and more resilient our community will be in a disaster. I look forward to seeing you on November 5th.
articles.title: Take 3 steps today to prepare for a wildfire

articles.text: Three Piedmont High School students, senior Gianna Yan, and juniors Siddarth Bhatia and Cleo Tahawi, were selected to serve as student school board members through June 30, 2023. They will be able to place “preferential votes,” to show their positions, but they will not be counted amongst the five elected board members’ votes on action items. In years prior, Associated Student Body (ASB) members gave reports to the board at the start of board meetings. The selection of official student members seeks to expand the role and impact of students upon board decisions and direction. They are scheduled to attend every regularly scheduled board meeting in-person and will have a weekly meeting with Superintendent Donald Evans to review each meeting’s agenda in advance. “We’re asking them to bring that information [from the meetings with Evans] back to the student body, and get some input, to actually bring the voice of the students to this governance team,” said Board President Cory Smegal. While he was superintendent at Berkeley Unified School District, Evans worked with student members, and has come with valuable experience to this new endeavor in Piedmont. Students were asked to submit applications by September 16, and after an administrative review, three applicants were selected for interviews. Smegal and board member Veronica Thigpen interviewed them with plans of picking one or two, but after interviews, decided to take all three for the task. “Four or five months ago I never saw myself sitting in city hall and actually seeing this happen,” said Gianna Yan at the September 28 board meeting. “It was more of a pipe dream [then], but now I am seeing it all come into fruition. Thank you so much.” Earlier in the evening Yan talked about some accessibility issues with the new “Academy” study hall period introduced this year at Piedmont and Millennium High. Bhatia and Tahawi spoke during the meeting as well and thanked the board for having been selected. Senior Gianna Yan Junior Siddarth Bhatia Junior Cleo Tahawi

Writing letters Does your favorite candy only have landfill destined wrapping? Write to the maker and ask them to change. articles.text: Candidates respond to questions Part five in a series With Election Day less than four weeks away the Piedmont Post has escalated its coverage of the two local elections, school board and city council. Starting this week and until the election on Tuesday November 8, this Candidate Q & A section will feature weekly answers from the school board candidates. Two questions are sent out on Thursday via email and candidates are instructed to limit their answers to under 150 words. SCHOOL BOARD Two open seats; three candidates. QUESTIONS – Week 5 1. Piedmont High School’s football team recently had to cancel its Homecoming football game. The team’s entire season is in jeopardy and the school’s 100-year-old program is in danger. What do you think needs to be done to continue the tradition, and how can you assist? 2. In February 2019, the School Board voted 4-1 against accepting $390,000 in federal funds to staff an armed police officer on campus. Do you see value in having an armed officer on campus? What is your view on campus safety? ment and our school district, but evidence points away from having an armed officer on campus. Instead, I support measures such as ensuring that doors are not propped open and that they lock, that students are protected even as they eat or play outside, and that we have drills with enough frequency so that students will know what to do even in the worst situation imaginable. Ongoing mental health support for our kids can also help them before problems escalate to violence. We want assurances that our children will be safe at school. Continuing to practice our safety protocols and procedures so our kids know what to do in an emergency is essential. RUCHI MEDHEKAR 1. Football program in jeopardy? First and foremost, I want our kids to be safe. I was worried when I heard about the season-ending injuries that occurred on the team, and my understanding is that the number of injuries on the roster drove the decision to cancel the game. I was very excited to hear that the school pivoted and showcased the girls’ volleyball game so that students could still participate in the Homecoming festivities. We’ve struggled with low participation in football at the high school level, but the numbers in middle school are promising and will likely feed the JV and Varsity teams in coming years. There are opportunities to collaborate with the Recreation Department to create early interest in sports. While I think it is important to appreciate our traditions, if students’ interests in sports are evolving, I believe our programs should meet the needs of our current students. 2. Campus Safety and Armed Officer on Campus? With every shooting - including the recent ones in Oakland and Thailand - the need to protect our students and keep our campuses safe becomes more pronounced and fraught. I appreciate the deep collaboration between our police departSHIRLEY HOOI 1. Football program in jeopardy? There is something special about the tradition of cheering on your local high school football team each fall season. It brings students, parents and the community together under the Friday night lights to revel in the hard work of the athletes and coaches on the field. The role of sports is principally to teach our kids invaluable life skills: physical and mental discipline, teamwork, leadership, resilience. Playing competitive sports builds character and allows them to experience a unique camaraderie in so doing, and all sports teams offer this opportunity. Students get to choose what sports they want to play, with their parents permission and support. My understanding is that increasingly, students are opting to play sports other than football, due to the risk of serious injury, and I fully support their decision, whatever that decision may be. 2. Campus Safety and Armed Officer on Campus? Improving student and staff safety is a paramount concern, and merits thoughtful reevaluation, particularly in light of the increasing number and severity of school shootings in the recent past. An SRO appears to be a promising way to both improve campus safety, as well as minimize the time for qualified law enforcement personnel to intercede - a key finding in the aftermath of the tragedy at Sandy Hook. That said, I am cognizant that even in our own District, concerns have been raised about this particular approach to improve safety. I am not sure what the right answer for PUSD is going forward, but I would find out by consulting all the key stakeholders to solicit inputs. Thereafter, I would carefully weigh the pros and cons in consultation with my fellow board members, and with a bias toward action to promote improved health and safety of our students and staff. LINDSAY THOMASSON 1. Football program in jeopardy? It is my understanding, based on conversations with football families, that the cancellation of the homecoming game and premature end to the season was the culmination of a number of factors. The varsity football team has few junior players due to the cancellation of practices during COVID; football was much slower to return than other sports. As players were injured, there wasn’t a sufficient number of substitutes and the team was forced to forfeit games. Fortunately, there is a very strong string of sophomore players, many of whom played in varsity games this year. There is also significant interest in middle school flag football which feeds into the high school football program. This, along with robust community support for high school sports, bodes well for the sustainability of the football program. Football Fridays are one of my favorite Piedmont traditions. It was incredibly disappointing for the entire community for the homecoming game to be canceled. Yet, I appreciate how the high school was able to change to a homecoming girls volleyball game instead, particularly given ongoing discussions about Title IX and recognition that girls sports should receive equal resources and recognition. 2. Campus Safety and Armed Officer on Campus? I reached out to Chief Bowers last month to discuss the relationship between the Piedmont Police Department and Piedmont School District. He explained that the relationship is generally collaborative and strong. However, he would like to see [the district] form a threat assessment team, something districts nationwide are implementing in an effort to identify and prevent violent incidents on school campuses. These multi-disciplinary teams are made up of police officers, school counselors, county mental health professionals, and teachers. The School Board, in conjunction with the district and PPD, should make establishment of a threat assessment team a priority; prevention should be our primary objective. I am unconvinced that an armed officer would make our campuses safer and may, counterintuitively, provide a false sense of security. We’re fortunate that PPD is centrally located in close proximity to our schools; they can and do respond quickly to issues that arise. That said, in addition to the creation of a threat response team, It is essential that we continually review our school safety plans and have regular earthquake, fire, and lockdown drills so that everyone on our school campuses is prepared to act quickly if an incident occurs.

articles.text: Screenagers is an award-winning documentary from 2016 by Delaney Ruston. Piedmont Parents Network (PPN) is showing the award-winning documentary, Screenagers: Growing Up in the Digital Age on Thursday, October 20 at 7:00 pm in the Middle School Multi-purpose room. The viewing and discussion afterwards are offered to all parents in the Piedmont community, as well as high school and middle school students. The event is in collaboration with Piedmont Middle School and the School District Wellness Center The 70-minute documentary follows physician and filmmaker Delaney Ruston as she probes into the vulnerable corners of family life, including her own, to explore struggles over social media, video games, academics and internet addiction. Through poignant, and unexpectedly funny stories, along with surprising insights from authors, psychologists, and brain scientists, the film reveals how tech time impacts kids’ development. It offers solutions on how adults can empower kids to best navigate the digital world and find balance. PPN invites parents to attend even if they have already seen the film, and as a community explore the impact of screens and social media. After the film, small group discussions will take place as PPN provides resources on how to find balance for children in the digital age. Parents and kids age 11 and older are encouraged to attend together. Seating is limited. Please RSVP at forms.gle/ LUw2nTKTfUukwbrj8 The presentation is the first of this year’s PMS Parent Engagement Nights – a series of regular events at the middle school as part of the Connected Learning Initiative. These events focus on issues and challenges facing families and students. PPN’s goal is to support and empower parents in raising kids who behave ethically, think critically, and participate safely and responsibly. PPN holds monthly gradelevel meetings in homes to discuss topics of interest to small parent groups, to include guest speakers. PPN also helps to keep communication lines open with middle school and high school administrators to ensure parent voices can be heard in a coordinated and constructive way. For information on joining Piedmont Parents Network, contact Edit Kincses (kincsesedit1@ gmail.com) or Caroline Santander (carolinesantander@gmail.com). articles.text: In creativity theory, there is a concept caked the 4C’s: Mini-C, Little-C, Pro-C and Big-C. The idea behind each one of these is that creativity within our society serves different purposes and functions. Big-C is talking about creativity through the work of individuals who have had a national and international impact on our culture, community, and society with their work. Pro-C is for those creators who are wellknown within their field and area of expertise and are at the top of their form. Little-C refers to the day-to-day act of creation that all of us can undertake – a song that is composed around a campfire, a painting that is for the enjoyment of the creator and a few friends on Instagram, a new creative idea for how to move along the pickup lane at school that helps a group of parents. And Mini-C is the creative process that sometimes doesn’t even leave our own minds or, if it does, it is purely for the process of learning and experimenting. In our families, we have the opportunity to engage with all of these different types of creativity on a daily basis. Play a Beethoven piece at dinner and you are experiencing and sharing Big-C. Attend a Bay Area Children’s Theatre production or take a class with a teaching artist and you are seeing Pro-C at work. Create an original piece of art with your child that tells the story of your family vacation and post it to your Whatsapp group; that is Try practicing the 4C’s of creativity at home. Little-C. And, look at the challenge of getting your kids out the door on time in the morning from a new perspective, or experiment with a different way to organize the bedtime routine; that is Mini-C. The key from my perspective is that we need all of these types of Creativity in our world. How can we expect to have new and exciting creators who become the Pro-C and Big-C thinkers of the future if we don’t encourage our kids to start to learn and fail and try again, in all sorts of different domains of creativity. How will they ever learn to do that if we don’t model that behavior? Try a family C inventory: • Are you engaging with all levels of creativity? • What easy and simple things could you add to your family activities or routines to incorporate any missing levels of creativity? • Do you talk about or use prod- • • • • • ucts that really big thinkers invented or created? Are mistakes and failing encouraged when trying new things? Do you model the joy of Little-C creativity by being proud of what you are making instead of letting our critical voice out and undermining our accomplishments? Do you have any Pro-C creators in your community? Have you asked them about their work and how they use creativity in their lives? Can you find more opportunities to listen/watch/engage with visual, performing, digital art? What types of creative activities do you all enjoy doing together? articles.text: ‘Twas the night of All Hallow’s Eve and Sally the witch of Salem was getting ready to enjoy a night of trick-or-treating, feeling the wind blow through her hair as she rode her broom and carved pumpkins with her cat Lucinda. Sally lived in the forest with her cat in a quaint cottage. Her cottage had remained the same and had been passed down from her ancestors who lived in Salem before her. It it was trapped in colonial times. None the less, Sally had made it ghostly and ready for All Hallow’s Eve. Carved pumpkins with candles inside lined the perimeter of her house to cast scary shadows on the ground. Sally also enchanted mini skeletons to dance on the roof of her house through the night. And last but not least, Sally decided to turn the smoke that came from her chimney a smoky green color for extra fright to anyone who might see it. As Sally was getting ready to get on her broom and fly over the town of Salem, she ran into a small problem. She couldn’t find her hat! Oh no, she cried, as she ran around her cottage in search of the most essential piece of her outfit. But the pointed black hat was nowhere to be found. Sally decided to retrace her steps to when she last saw it. She took Lucinda and put her in the pet basket attached to her broom that she had bought at Brooms and Things Emporium, exclusively for witches who need pet accessories for brooms, and took off into the sunset in the direction of the main part of Salem. Sally f lew as fast as her broom could take her, almost breaking the speed limit allowed for brooms. She landed in front of Styles and Creams, the onestop shop for every mysterious baked good and every spooktacular dress that came straight from Milan Witch and Wizard Fashion Week. Sally ran in, out of breath looking for her hat. She looked on every shelf, through every rack of clothes, and every cake case that she could get her hands on. But no such luck. Her fellow witches even helped her look for the hat, because every witch knows how important a black pointed hat is. But after 15 minutes of frantically searching, Sally gave up. Until she remembered there was one last place she could look for her hat, Merlin’s Potion Palace, the most famous potion brewery on the planet. Well not really. The actual title of most famous on the planet was held by some wizard named Nicholas Flammel who had his own potion brewery in England. (But Merlin’s Potion Palace made one mean Time Reverser draught. It comes in handy when you’re running late.) She had been there earlier that day to get the potion that would turn her fire and smoke green. This time Sally walked in, heels clicking and wood creaking on the ancient floors. The hut itself was operated by no one, but ask and you shall receive whatever you need. Every corner was covered in different potions for different occasions. And lo and behold. There on the counter of the dark and musty brewery, sat her hat. Sally couldn’t contain hers excitement and ran straight for her hat. Hugging it as soon as it was in her hands. Lucinda wrapped herself around Sally’s ankles purring in satisfaction that the hat was found. Sally and Lucinda proudly left the potion brewery and hopped on the broom and started their journey back home to the edge of the forest. The night of All Hallow’s Eve had a full moon. As Sally flew, she noticed that she would be flying through the middle of the moon with her witch’s outline visible to everyone looking to the sky. But Sally decided, what, after all, is Halloween without some spooky witch sightings to be reported. And with that she flew through the middle of the moon, pointy hat and all. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and a sophomore at the Bentley School.
articles.title: HALLOWEEN SPECIAL The mystery of the disappearing black hat

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, October 12, 2022 Thinking Outside the Classroom Creativity on a little and big scale By Nina Meehan In creativity theory, there is a concept caked the 4C’s: Mini-C, Little-C, Pro-C and Big-C. The idea behind each one of these is that creativity within our society serves different purposes and functions. Big-C is talking about creativity through the work of individuals who have had a national and international impact on our culture, community, and society with their work. Pro-C is for those creators who are wellknown within their field and area of expertise and are at the top of their form. Little-C refers to the day-to-day act of creation that all of us can undertake – a song that is composed around a campfire, a painting that is for the enjoyment of the creator and a few friends on Instagram, a new creative idea for how to move along the pickup lane at school that helps a group of parents. And Mini-C is the creative process that sometimes doesn’t even leave our own minds or, if it does, it is purely for the process of learning and experimenting. In our families, we have the opportunity to engage with all of these different types of creativity on a daily basis. Play a Beethoven piece at dinner and you are experiencing and sharing Big-C. Attend a Bay Area Children’s Theatre production or take a class with a teaching artist and you are seeing Pro-C at work. Create an original piece of art with your child that tells the story of your family vacation and post it to your Whatsapp group; that is Try practicing the 4C’s of creativity at home. Little-C. And, look at the challenge of getting your kids out the door on time in the morning from a new perspective, or experiment with a different way to organize the bedtime routine; that is Mini-C. The key from my perspective is that we need all of these types of Creativity in our world. How can we expect to have new and exciting creators who become the Pro-C and Big-C thinkers of the future if we don’t encourage our kids to start to learn and fail and try again, in all sorts of different domains of creativity. How will they ever learn to do that if we don’t model that behavior? Try a family C inventory: • Are you engaging with all levels of creativity? • What easy and simple things could you add to your family activities or routines to incorporate any missing levels of creativity? • Do you talk about or use prod- • • • • • ucts that really big thinkers invented or created? Are mistakes and failing encouraged when trying new things? Do you model the joy of Little-C creativity by being proud of what you are making instead of letting our critical voice out and undermining our accomplishments? Do you have any Pro-C creators in your community? Have you asked them about their work and how they use creativity in their lives? Can you find more opportunities to listen/watch/engage with visual, performing, digital art? What types of creative activities do you all enjoy doing together? Nina Meehan is the CEO and Founder of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. Sally lived in the forest with her cat in a quaint cottage. Her cottage had remained the same and had been passed down from her ancestors who lived in Salem before her. It it was trapped in colonial times. None the less, Sally had made it ghostly and ready for All Hallow’s Eve. Carved pumpkins with candles inside lined the perimeter of her house to cast scary shadows on the ground. Sally also enchanted mini skeletons to dance on the roof of her house through the night. And last but not least, Sally decided to turn the smoke that came from her chimney a smoky green color for extra fright to anyone who might see it. As Sally was getting ready to get on her broom and fly over the town of Salem, she ran into a small problem. She couldn’t find her hat! Oh no, she cried, as she ran around her cottage in search of the most essential piece of her outfit. But the pointed black hat was nowhere to be found. Sally decided to retrace her steps to when she last saw it. She took Lucinda and put her in the pet basket attached to her broom that she had bought at Brooms and Things Emporium, exclusively for witches who need pet accessories for brooms, and took off into the sunset in the direction of the main part of Salem. Sally f lew as fast as her broom could take her, almost breaking the speed limit allowed for brooms. She landed in front of Styles and Creams, the onestop shop for every mysterious baked good and every spooktacular dress that came straight from Milan Witch and Wizard Fashion Week. Sally ran in, out of breath looking for her hat. She looked on every shelf, through every rack of clothes, and every cake case that she could get her hands on. But no such luck. Her fellow witches even helped her look for the hat, because every witch knows how important a black pointed hat is. But after 15 minutes of frantically searching, Sally gave up. Until she remembered there was one last place she could look for her hat, Merlin’s Potion Palace, the most famous potion brewery on the planet. Well not really. The actual title of most famous on the planet was held by some wizard named Nicholas Flammel who had his own potion brewery in England. (But Merlin’s Potion Palace made one mean Time Reverser draught. It comes in handy when you’re running late.) She had been there earlier that day to get the potion that would turn her fire and smoke green. This time Sally walked in, heels clicking and wood creaking on the ancient floors. The hut itself was operated by no one, but ask and you shall receive whatever you need. Every corner was covered in different potions for different occasions. And lo and behold. There on the counter of the dark and musty brewery, sat her hat. Sally couldn’t contain hers excitement and ran straight for her hat. Hugging it as soon as it was in her hands. Lucinda wrapped herself around Sally’s ankles purring in satisfaction that the hat was found. Sally and Lucinda proudly left the potion brewery and hopped on the broom and started their journey back home to the edge of the forest. The night of All Hallow’s Eve had a full moon. As Sally flew, she noticed that she would be flying through the middle of the moon with her witch’s outline visible to everyone looking to the sky. But Sally decided, what, after all, is Halloween without some spooky witch sightings to be reported. And with that she flew through the middle of the moon, pointy hat and all. Most Critical Fiscal Issues The RHNA allocation is about to be a critical fiscal issue for our city. Adding 587 new rental units will equate to approximately 1761 new residents for one-bedroom units. Housing laws allow for two people per bedroom plus one. Conservatively, this equates to approximately a 19% or more increase to the city’s population. The impact on our schools, police services, fire services, etc. will be astronomical. The overwhelming cost of these services will fall on the taxpaying residents. Is it fair to ask our residents to pay for these services? Twenty-eight percent or more of the new housing units must be allocated to those with extremely low income, less than $69,000 annually. Most applicants lack adequate income and the credit score needed to secure housing. I have been very creative in finding ways to house these people. Over the years I have worked diligently with the HUD VASH and Oakland Housing Authority. I have made homes for many veterans and homeless people. I understand the Housing Choice Voucher program very well. In 2018, my husband and I were presented with an Award of Recognition from the Oakland Housing Authority for having housed many tenants in need. My experience in this area is vast and will add great value to the city council as we move forward to add affordable housing units to our city. NANCY BOSTROM 1. The prudent management of the massive pool project. When a full-sized 160 foot by 85 foot pool with 10 lanes costs between $300,000.00 -$500,000.00, I wonder if this one includes a 150 foot yacht, Sikorsky helicopter, a polo field, stable and a petting zoo. The social, ecological and massive financial costs lurking ahead related to the expenses of housing, protecting, educating and policing an additional 1200 citizens, their 2400 cars and 2,400+ children is like asking Oakland to support another 100,000 people, except that Oakland is space-rich, without touching their 1,000’s of acres of parkland. Each new fireman, our first responders, will cost $300,000. City Hall must be rebuilt. ADU’s are best strategy, but any new housing is least disruptive on Grand Avenue. 2. Relevant Life Experience I have lived in Piedmont in the same house almost all my life except when I was away at boarding school. I graduated from Piedmont High School and was in all the plays and most of the clubs. All students and teachers deserve a learning environment away from fear, which is why the gun issue is so vital. I have traveled all of my life. My family were obsessed birders and art collectors. I have seen the massive populations of Calcutta, Africa, Bangladesh; I never expected to see Oakland have third world Hoovervilles. Small affordable units people can own is the answer, not million dollar apartments. BRIDGET HARRIS 1. Most Critical Fiscal Issues Piedmont’s most critical fiscal issue is the renovation of Police and Fire facilities which was delayed because of Measure UU. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, October 12, 2022 By Jay Russell Part five in a series With Election Day less than four weeks away the Piedmont Post has escalated its coverage of the two local elections, school board and city council. Two questions are sent out on Thursday via email and candidates are instructed to limit their answers to under 150 words. CITY COUNCIL Three open seats; six candidates QUESTIONS – Week 5 1. From your perspective, what are some of the most critical fiscal issues facing Piedmont now and in the near future? 2. Please expand on how a specific experience in your life has prepared you to serve on city council. TOM RAMSEY 1. Most Critical Fiscal Issues Here are three issues: Maintenance: Piedmont’s budget report this year identified that our maintenance fund does not include allocations for necessary capital improvement projects for the Fire Department / City Hall, the Police Department, Veterans Hall, the Recreation Building, and Parks. Pool: Local construction cost indexes forecast a +15% yearover-year increase in construction costs by year-end 2022. - or since our budget was determined for the pool. We need to continue our fiscal responsibility and monitor pension costs closely. 2. Relevant Life Experience I sometimes joke that my seven years on the Planning Commission have made my skin thicker. articles.text: Beats James Logan, Foothill & California Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team continued its strong season with three wins in four games at the Tri-Valley Tournament at Foothill High in Pleasanton last weekend, October 7-8. articles.text: Piedmont‘s tennis team took firm control of the Western Alameda County Conference title race on Thursday, October 6 at the Berkeley Tennis Club, defeating Berkeley High in a narrow 4-3 match day. The win improves Piedmont’s record to 10-3 overall; they remain undefeated in league at 6-0. PHS’ last remaining opponent on the league schedule is Bishop O’Dowd, who they defeated 4-2 at the California Tennis Classic in Fresno on September 10. Thursday’s win came down to the No. 1 doubles, which Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini won in three sets with a decisive 6-0 victory in the decisive set/ The scores with Berkeley’s Rowna Kenneth and Malika Treyna were 6-2, 2-6, 6-0. “The Berkeley match was very exciting. It came down to the last match on the court with Mara and Miki. They split sets and at the start of the third set, the Berkeley player mishit an overhead smash and the ball unfortunately hit Mara in the back. I started to award the point to the Berkeley team when Corey [Reich, assistant coach] signaled that the Berkeley girl’s follow through hit the net for a Piedmont point. After that, it seemed like our girls barely lost another point,” said coach Jim Landes. The final set by the doubles team was characterized with outstanding play at the net by both LaForte and Bini with several well-placed volleys, including a match-winner by Bini to close out the day. “We re-focused after that second set and won 6-0. This was our fourth match together this year, but we played freshman year together and then we both played singles. Now we’re reunited as seniors and we’re happier than ever,” said LaForte. “The thing with tennis is that its super easy to get in your head and that digs a hole. We were both getting really frustrated in the second set and it felt like we forgot how to play tennis. And then we woke up,” mentioned Bini. Match Recap Piedmont started the day with a 6-3, 6-2 win at No. 3 doubles with Sophia Kalamas and Arianna Kortum and went ahead by two matches with a 7-6 (6-1), 6-0 win at No. 2 doubles with Kate Jumper and Cecilia DeFazio. But then Berkeley won the next three matches to jump ahead 3-2 with each match going three sets. No. 3 singles Carolina Romanczuk lost 6-1, 2-6, 6-3. Anne Jumper at No. 2 singles fell 4-6, 6-4, 6-3. At No. 4 singles, Annika Gilliland lost 6-7 (7-5), 6-3, 6-2. Tanya Kononov a, Piedmont’s No. 1, had an easy 6-0, 6-2 win to bring the team score even at 3-3. At No. 1 doubles, LaForte and Bini won handily in the first set 6-2 but lost their mojo in the second set in a 6-2 loss. Then, the duo shut out the Berkeley doubles team in the third set for a final score of 6-2, 2-6, 6-0. articles.text: Editor: I read Jon Comeaux’s “Reflecting on the lifeline of Piedmont’s football program” in the October 5th issue of the Post, in which he summarizes the last 10 years of Piedmont High football. I have coached PHS freshmen and JV football teams for 17 years, so I am familiar with this history. Jon is correct that the football program has struggled over the last two seasons. This is because of low levels of participation by the classes of 2021 (last year’s graduates), 2022 (this year’s seniors), and 2023 (this year’s juniors). There are probably a number of reasons for the low levels, but an important one is that interest in football by middle school boys was not sufficiently cultivated in the recent years before 2020. However, a very good thing happened two years ago for Piedmont football and Piedmont students when the Recreation Department engaged Billy Goldstein and his Skyhawks youth sports program to operate the middle school flag football program. There are 19 sophomores on Piedmont’s football teams this year in large part because of the interest in football that Goldstein’s program generated. There are also 14 current freshmen on the JV team this year, most of whom have participated in the middle school program. The numbers of freshmen and sophomores on this year’s team are solid. It is important that middle school students continue to be exposed to football, so that they want to play in the future. Happily, the football program with Skyhawks continues. There are 68 middle school students participating in the Skyhawks program this fall, and many of them will play PHS football. It is important that there not be a negative perception regarding the future of Piedmont football. A false perception can become reality, if people believe it. Over the next two years, there will be a resurgence of Piedmont High football. The current sophomores are an especially strong class and the classes that are following it are going to be good, too. It is important that Piedmont students have the opportunity to play football because they can benefit greatly from the experience. It is the hardest thing most of them have ever done. My two sons were not great football players, but they played all four years at PHS. Doing so, gave them the confidence that they could accomplish other hard things in life. Football made them stronger and helped them become the fine men they are. Future generations of Piedmont boys must have the same opportunity. –Dick Carter

articles.text: With making mention of the current athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, it can get easy to lose track of those who have continued their careers after moving on from the small town in the hills. In this article, we take a look at four former Piedmont Post Athletes of the Year who are currently active at the collegiate level this fall season, including distance runners Ellie Black, Jack Stein, and Sophia Zalewski, along with tennis star Makenna Thiel. Ellie Black, University of California Ellie Black, PHS Class of 2022 and the Post’s 2022 Athlete of the Year, is continuing her strong start to her collegiate career with the UC Berkeley cross-country team. She was the top runner for Cal in their most recent event at the UC Riverside Invitational on September 17 and finished 31st of 265 runners. In Cal’s season-opener at the University of San Francisco Invitational at Golden Gate Park on September 3, Black was also her team’s lead runner, fniishing 22nd of 125 runners with a time of 22:03.8. The Golden Bears finished eighth of 13 teams. Cal’s head coach Bobby Lockhart had high praise of Black after her run in Riverside. “Ellie Black keeps impressing us,” Lockhart said. “She’s just getting going, and I see no reason she won’t continue to make significant jumps.” Photo by Walter Teitelbaum Ellie Black, the Posts’ 2022 Athlete of the Year, is leading the charge on the California Golden Bears’ cross country program. Jack Stein, Pomona-Pitzer College Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, also earned the Post’s Athlete of the Year award in June along with Black. He’s been a big part of the Pomona-Pitzer Sagehens’ cross country team’s first four meets this season. Most recently at the Pomona-Pitzer Invitational on October 8, Stein was the third best runner for his college by finishing 29th of 163 runners with a time of 26:09.1. articles.text: Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Gardens at Lake Merritt, returns tomorrow, Thursday, October 13. The festival has drawn more than 10,000 art and nature enthusiasts to Lake Merritt since 2012. The festival celebrates its 11th anniversary this year for three nights, October 13-15. Patrons will experience 60 locally produced illuminated art displays throughout Oakland’s seven-acre municipal gardens. The event includes a kids’ “fun zone,” art market, food court, and a beer and wine garden. The Festival is hosted by the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a volunteer organization The annual Autumn Lights Festival at Lake Merritt. formed in 2004. The nonprofit partners with the City of Oakland to enhance the seven-acre collection of themed gardens in Oakland and on the shores of Lake Merritt. The volunteer organization maintains a bonsai garden, a Sensory Garden, a Toddler Garden, an Urban Edible Garden, and more at Lake Merritt. Tickets are on sale now and may be purchased by visiting https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/ autumn-lights-festival-2022/.
articles.title: Autumn Lights Festival returns to Lake Merritt this weekend

articles.text: Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside. Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside recently was named ‘Best Attraction’ in the U.S. by the Dutch international travel and tourism company Tiqets. The annual awards have served as a tool for helping discerning travelers since 2017. Tiqets’ sixth annual Remarkable Venue Awards program recognizes the best museums and attractions in the world in seven categories, from the best hidden gems to the most remarkable venues. More than 200 nominees competed worldwide to be recognized in the coveted travel awards. The 2022 winners represent the best of the tourism industry. Seven total venues in the U.S. received top honors, including: • Best Attraction: Filoli Historic House & Garden, California’s Bay Area • Best Onsite Experience: Musical Instrument Museum, Phoenix • Best Museum: The National WWII Museum, New Orleans • Most Innovative Venue: Area 15, Las Vegas • Most Remarkable Venue: Titanic Museum Attraction Pigeon Forge, Tennessee • Best Landmark: SUMMIT • One Vanderbilt, New York City Best Hidden Gem: Fotografiska, New York Winners from eight other countries were also announced, including in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, the UAE, and the UK. Voting is currently underway now through October 19 for the Filoli Historic House & Garden to be named as a Global Winner in the same category. To cast your vote, visit: https://www.tiqets. com/blog/best-museums-attractions-in-2022/. The Tiqets Awards The Remarkable Venue Awards celebrate seven categories of awards in nine countries worldwide. Since 2017, the awards have recognised museums and attractions in France, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States. For the first time this year the awards program will include Germany, Portugal and the United Arab Emirates. articles.text: Live concert by hometown orchestra at PCA on November 6 Piedmont hometown orchestra is presenting a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon, November 6, at 4 p.m. Performing a varied and unusual program, the orchestra will be conducted by Martha Stoddard and Sue Crum. The rarely heard Overture to Johann Albrecht’s comedy Der Teufel als Hydraulicus, composed by Franz Schubert when he was just 14, opens the concert, followed by the delightful Romanian Dances, by Bela Bartok. As a special audience treat, the humorous Ferdinand the Bull, by American author Munro Leaf and based upon the children’s story of the same name, will be performed by violinist Joseph Gold with narration by Piedmont native and City Council member Betsy Andersen. It is the story of a bull who would rather smell the flowers than fight in bullfights. The work was banned by both Hitler and the Spanish Fascists as “degenerate democratic propaganda.” The program concludes with Mozart’s orchestral masterpiece, his Symphony No. 40 in G minor, composed during some of the artist’s darkest days but finding its way from the turbulence of the beginning sections into the triumph of the conclusion. Tickets at the door are $20 cash or credit card. Doors open at 3:30 p.m. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at Bonita Avenue. Street parking is available.

articles.text: Larry Carlton was born in Torrance in Southern California in 1948 and began guitar lessons at age six. He was introduced to jazz in junior high school after hearing The Gerald Wilson Big Band album, Moment of Truth, with Joe Pass on guitar. It led him to explore jazz by other guitarists, including Barney Kessel, Wes Montgomery and B.B. King. Larry’s first professional gig was at a supper club in 1962. He honed his guitar-playing skills in the clubs and studios of greater Los Angeles. In 1968 through 1970, he toured with the Fifth Dimension and did studio sessions with Vikki Carr, Andy Williams and the Partridge Family. Then he joined the Crusaders. “I got a call to do a session for Donovan, and when I showed up, Joe Sample, the Crusaders’ keyboard player, was already there,” recalled Carlton. “I plugged in and joined Joe on a downbeat he played, and right away we had a moment of musical communication. Monday morning my phone rang, and it was the Crusaders’ office saying, ‘The guys are in the studio starting an album. Can you come in and join them for the next two weeks?’” Larry was invited to join the Crusaders and played on 13 of their albums from 1971 through 1976. Joni Mitchell’s Court and Spark album, the first record she made with a rhythm section, disGuitarist Larry Carlton plays Carlton’s distinctive technique – a style Mitchell referred to as “fly fishing”, which is interesting because Larry actually enjoys fly fishing. Larry did more than 3000 studio sessions by the early 1980’s, including with Steely Dan, Linda Rondstadt, Michael Jackson and Bobby Blue Bland. Other significant studio session players included Steve Cropper, Tommy Tedesco, Chet Atkins, Steve Lukather, Glen Campbell, Lee Ritenour and Brent Mason. Larry’s catalog of work includes film soundtracks, television themes and work on over 100 gold albums. Larry won four Grammy Awards: Theme from Hill Street Blues, 1981; Minute by Minute, 1987; No Substitutions: Live in Osaka, 2001 and his album Take Your Pick, 2010. In his early years, Larry mostly played a Gibson 335 guitar. In the late seventies, he built a home studio, which he named “Room 335” (also the name of one of his compositions). In the seventies, his nickname was “Mr. 335”. Since the late seventies, Larry phased out studio session work and transitioned to recording his own albums, his focus ever since. Then he joined the Crusaders. “I got a call to do a session for Donovan, and when I showed up, Joe Sample, the Crusaders’ keyboard player, was already there,” recalled Carlton. “I plugged in and joined Joe on a downbeat he played, and right away we had a moment of musical communication. Monday morning my phone rang, and it was the Crusaders’ office saying, ‘The guys are in the studio starting an album. Can you come in and join them for the next two weeks?’” Larry was invited to join the Crusaders and played on 13 of their albums from 1971 through 1976. Joni Mitchell’s Court and Spark album, the first record she made with a rhythm section, disGuitarist Larry Carlton plays Carlton’s distinctive technique – a style Mitchell referred to as “fly fishing”, which is interesting because Larry actually enjoys fly fishing. Larry did more than 3000 studio sessions by the early 1980’s, including with Steely Dan, Linda Rondstadt, Michael Jackson and Bobby Blue Bland. Other significant studio session players included Steve Cropper, Tommy Tedesco, Chet Atkins, Steve Lukather, Glen Campbell, Lee Ritenour and Brent Mason. Larry’s catalog of work includes film soundtracks, television themes and work on over 100 gold albums. Larry won four Grammy Awards: Theme from Hill Street Blues, 1981; Minute by Minute, 1987; No Substitutions: Live in Osaka, 2001 and his album Take Your Pick, 2010. In his early years, Larry mostly played a Gibson 335 guitar. In the late seventies, he built a home studio, which he named “Room 335” (also the name of one of his compositions). In the seventies, his nickname was “Mr. 335”. Since the late seventies, Larry phased out studio session work and transitioned to recording his own albums, his focus ever since. Many of the works come from their outings in the high Sierras where they regularly hike and take their painting materials and easels in backpacks. Often the smaller works are used to create bigger paintings, giving the artists the opportunity to explore their subjects on a larger scale. This show also has local themes such as seascapes from the Monterey Peninsula, Bay Area gardens, some still life works, and a few portraits. “We find working together in wild areas with rich landscape to be a transcendent experience. We feel very fortunate to be able to explore and create from the incredible beauty of California,” said David. articles.text: Russian-American author Anastasia Edel, a Piedmont resident, will present a 4-week illustrated lecture titled Russia’s War on Ukraine, with classes starting on Thursday, October 20 at 2:30 p.m. The course is being offered by Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at the University of California in Berkeley, where Edel conducted an eight-week illustrated lecture in 2018 on Understanding Russia, a course that intertwines the country’s political and cultural developments with historical perspectives expressed in film, music, and literature. The last four years have proven to be a busy time for Edel. In 2018 she gave the keynote address at OLLI and to the League of Women Voters in Piedmont on The State of US-Russian Relations. One year later she delivered talks at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco, the University of Washington, and Berkeley City Club Due in part to the publicity generated by op ed pieces she wrote for the New York Times between February and May this year, she was an invited commentators on CNN MSNBC and Bay Area NBC. In the past five years, six of her guest essays an opinion pieces have appeared in the New York Times, with a spike of interest since Russia began its move to wage war on neighboring Ukraine. The course fee for Russia’s War on Ukraine through OLLI is $90 for the four lectures, each of which will be from 2:30 to 4:00 p.m. on consecutive Thursdays, October 20 to November 10. The course will stream live on the scheduled day and time and will also be recorded. Videos will be available on Friday each week. When Russian missiles struck multiple cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine in February 2020, Russia became an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common past. How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And where does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? Edel provided some perspective on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine earlier this year with a lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in April. To register for the current course, click on: https://olli.berkeley.edu/programs/courses/russia%E2%80%99s-war-ukraine. Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel is an acclaimed writer, social historian, and New York Times contributor. She’s the author of “Russia: Putin’s Playground,” a concise guide to Russian history, politics and culture.

articles.text: A turnout of 14 members of the First Mondays Reading group met on October 3 to discuss Unlikely Allies, by Joel Richard Paul. Participating were Phil Witte, Jerry Gragg, Mike Henn, Laura Goldman, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Martin Levy, Bella Almanzan, Adrienne Hamlin, Peggy Rourke, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The author is a professor and associate dean at the University of California’s Hastings College of Law, who recounts a true story of how three men used espionage, betrayal, and sexual deception to obtain France’s help for the colonies in the American Revolution. Silas Deane was a Connecticut merchant and delegate to the Continental Congress. Caron de Beaumarchais was a successful playwright who wrote the librettos for The Barber of Seville and The Marriage of Figaro. Chevalier d’Eon, was a flamboyant and mysterious officer, diplomat, and spy. He had incriminating documents against Louis XVI that helped obtain a crucial Franco-American alliance. The gender of d’Eon was a mystery until the end of the book. Paul’s story is different from what most of the readers learned in school about our Founding Fathers, who, we are told, were not saints endowed with wisdom, moral character, and virtue. Washington is “painfully aware of his own limitations as a military commander.” Samuel Adams is the head of a self-serving political faction. Ethan Allen is a scoundrel. Thomas Paine is a libeler. Benjamin Franklin likes to bounce pretty women on his knee, and the Lees of Virginia are more interested in nepotism than victory. Paul has no hesitation with these representations. “By placing the founders of our nation on a pedestal, we risk setting up an impossible standard for future generations to follow.” For the author, Silas Deane is one of the few selfless characters in the American Revolution. His tireless efforts cost him his fortune, family life, and reputation. Additionally, his doubts about the Americans’ ability to win the war, and his belief that a treaty should be negotiated with Britain, cost him dearly. While the book’s content deals with important historical matters, many of the readers found the book to be a struggle. It was educational, but not particularly entertaining for them. There were too many characters. A common reader complaint was that the book needed a better editor. They felt there was too much detail that detracted from important storylines. However, some readers enjoyed the book, which provides an important historical understanding of why France supported the American Revolution. It was not because the French king believed in democracy, but rather it was his desire to weaken his rival, Great Britain. The honest portrayals of our Founding Fathers with their imperfections is important to understand. The group appreciated Paul showing that political divisions existed among the Founding Fathers, and that and that political polarization is not new. The question of how appropriate the U.S. Constitution is today was raised. Is it outdated and should it be replaced with a new one? The group agreed that Unlikely Allies, like the Founding Fathers, might not be perfect, but the book did provide a more complete understanding of the creation of our country, and thus has value. With their discussion complete the readers considered their next books. They had previously selected Klara and the Sun by Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro for November, and after some back and forth discussions, the readers picked the non-fiction Priestdaddy by Patricia Lockwood for December, and Afterparties by Anthony Veasna So for January. The group’s next meeting will be November 7 at 1:30 p.m. at the Tea House. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Registration is required by calling the Recreation Department at 510-420-3070.

First Monday Readers dive into Unlikely Allies By Dick Carter A turnout of 14 members of the First Mondays Reading group met on October 3 to discuss Unlikely Allies, by Joel Richard Paul. Participating were Phil Witte, Jerry Gragg, Mike Henn, Laura Goldman, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Martin Levy, Bella Almanzan, Adrienne Hamlin, Peggy Rourke, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The author is a professor and associate dean at the University of California’s Hastings College of Law, who recounts a true story of how three men used espionage, betrayal, and sexual deception to obtain France’s help for the colonies in the American Revolution. Silas Deane was a Connecticut merchant and delegate to the Continental Congress. Caron de Beaumarchais was a successful playwright who wrote the librettos for The Barber of Seville and The Marriage of Figaro. Chevalier d’Eon, was a flamboyant and mysterious officer, diplomat, and spy. He had incriminating documents against Louis XVI that helped obtain a crucial Franco-American alliance. The gender of d’Eon was a mystery until the end of the book. Paul’s story is different from what most of the readers learned in school about our Founding Fathers, who, we are told, were not saints endowed with wisdom, moral character, and virtue. Washington is “painfully aware of his own limitations as a military commander.” Samuel Adams is the head of a self-serving political faction. Ethan Allen is a scoundrel. Thomas Paine is a libeler. Benjamin Franklin likes to bounce pretty women on his knee, and the Lees of Virginia are more interested in nepotism than victory. Paul has no hesitation with these representations. “By placing the founders of our nation on a pedestal, we risk setting up an impossible standard for future generations to follow.” For the author, Silas Deane is one of the few selfless characters in the American Revolution. His tireless efforts cost him his fortune, family life, and reputation. Additionally, his doubts about the Americans’ ability to win the war, and his belief that a treaty should be negotiated with Britain, cost him dearly. While the book’s content deals with important historical matters, many of the readers found the book to be a struggle. It was educational, but not particularly entertaining for them. There were too many characters. A common reader complaint was that the book needed a better editor. They felt there was too much detail that detracted from important storylines. However, some readers enjoyed the book, which provides an important historical understanding of why France supported the American Revolution. It was not because the French king believed in democracy, but rather it was his desire to weaken his rival, Great Britain. The honest portrayals of our Founding Fathers with their imperfections is important to understand. The group appreciated Paul showing that political divisions existed among the Founding Fathers, and that and that political polarization is not new. The question of how appropriate the U.S. Constitution is today was raised. Is it outdated and should it be replaced with a new one? The group agreed that Unlikely Allies, like the Founding Fathers, might not be perfect, but the book did provide a more complete understanding of the creation of our country, and thus has value. With their discussion complete the readers considered their next books. They had previously selected Klara and the Sun by Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro for November, and after some back and forth discussions, the readers picked the non-fiction Priestdaddy by Patricia Lockwood for December, and Afterparties by Anthony Veasna So for January. articles.text: Weekly training tips for the Thanksgiving morning 5K run Last week kicked off the official Piedmont Turkey Trot training plan, but there is still time to join in the training. Runner Jessica Freeman, a past winner of the Trot, has developed a weekly training plan for beginners to train specifically for the upcoming 5K on Thanksgiving Day, November 24th. The full training plan can be seen on the race website, piedmontturkeytrot.com. This week we will be adding in a speed workout which is best done at the track. Head over to Witter Field during non-school hours and run 2 fast laps. You want to be running at a pace that feels uncomfortable and you can hear yourself breathing, but not so fast that you can’t make it all the way around the track without stopping. For those new to the track, During the 2018 Turkey Trot, runners fly down Craig Avenue knowing they are within a quarter mile of the finish line. each full circle around the track is called a lap and it is 400 meters, or one-quarter of a mile in length. You should always run counterclockwise and it is most common to start your lap on the start line which is indicated by big bold numbers on the track. If you are standing in the stadium at Witter, you can see the start line on the right side. It is also best to start in the closest lane to the field (Lane 1). Don’t forget to warm up and cool down the body with a slow jog. Have fun out there! WEEK DAY WORKOUT October 10 Monday Run 1 min, Walk 1 min. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, October 12, 2022 By Ellie Somers and Troop 31318 Volunteers Piedmont Girl Scouts in Daisy Troop 31318 have started their second year off strong, with community service projects with an environmental focus. On the heels of a hugely successful beach cleanup at Jack London Aquatic Center for the 74th Annual California Coastal Clean Up Day, the girls have turned their attention to Piedmont’s own streets and trash cans. Comprised of 19 girls ages 6 and 7 from Havens and Wildwood schools, Troop 31318 has a plan for reducing the waste created during Halloween. The girls will have a Zero Waste recycling box outside Mulberry’s Market for one week before Halloween and one week after. Formed in 2021, Troop 31318 was largely unable to participate in community service the past two years due to ongoing COVID concerns. This year the girls have been excited to have a chance to get out in the greater community to increase their positive impact. After recent Troop meetings centered around reducing waste, Girl Scouts planning Green Halloween reusing items that have life left in them, and composting and recycling as much as possible, the girls are excited to introduce their candy wrapper recycling program to the community. With an expected start date of October 24, the Scouts are hoping to prevent the usual uptick in candy wrappers blowing around on streets at Halloween. TerraCycle’s Zero Waste boxes divert items that would otherwise end up in landfill, or in our streets and waterways, into specialized recycling facilities. Troop 31318 Scouts are hoping the community will take this opportunity to be thoughtful about its plastic-based waste. For trick or treating on Halloween, they urge handing out candy with compostable paperbased wrappers, such as candy that comes in small cardboard boxes. Please look for Troop 31318’s TerraCycle box outside Mulberry’s Market and consider saving your wrappers by participating in an important lesson in civic engagement and environmental responsibility for these young Scouts. I am proud to be treasurer of her school board campaign, and I encourage you to vote for Lindsay. –Cindy Hinman Medhekar – a commitment to academic excellence Editor: We write to urge Piedmont residents to vote for Ruchi Medhekar for PUSD School Board. Ruchi’s extensive service to the Piedmont community and Piedmont schools over the years makes her incredibly well qualified and exemplifies her dedication to our town. Her commitment to academic excellence and strong collaboration skills can be seen from her years of volunteerism, including serving as room parent to vice president and then president of the Beach Parents Organization, to the Tri-School Site Council, the Local Control and Accountability Plan (LCAP) Committee, and to the district’s Budget Advisory Committee. If that wasn’t enough, Ruchi also serves on the Board of the Piedmont Education Foundation and the Piedmont Recreation Commission. Ruchi is the PUSD board member that we very much need. Rob had the pleasure of serving with Ruchi during the 2021- 2022 school year as a member of the Budget Advisory Committee and the Parcel Tax Subcommittee. Ruchi’s commitment, diligence, budget and financial acumen, willingness to ask the tough questions and challenge assumptions, as well as her strengths as a collaborator, team builder and solution finder all showcase why Ruchi would be an incredible asset to the PUSD School Board.. We encourage everyone to consider her candidacy. Please vote for Ruchi Medhekar on November 8. –Rob Phillips & Elisa Lee Candidates who tick all the boxes Editor: We live in a town with a wealth of talent and we are very lucky to have people who want to step up and volunteer for important civic positions. The work is hard. These volunteers have to listen respectfully to myriad opinions, work in partnership with many different stakeholders, pay careful attention to the regulatory landscape, and, ultimately, think holistically to make a lot of decisions that range from routine to especially thorny. I’ve done a lot of hiring in my career and there are four criteria I look for to make a successful hire: relevant work experience, capacity to learn, ability to be collegial and collaborative, and no bullies or creeps (see the Robert Sutton book for the more colorful reference). I use this same list when I vote. For me, the candidates who score highest in all my criteria are: Betsy Anderson, Jennifer Long, and Tom Ramsay for city council; and Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson for school board. My husband and I have been in Piedmont for almost 25 years and I’m about to end my tenure on the school board after nine years. I know these candidates because I’ve worked with them or have watched them at work. To a person, they are smart, insightful, measured, respectful, and collaborative. They have significant skills from their professional and volunteer work that will serve us. They are thoughtful servant leaders who will ask good questions and will seek to find the best solutions given the many competing interests/viewpoints and the complex regulatory landscape. These candidates are who I would like to see lead us in the next four years, who will honor the work and responsibility, and will be respectful of the offices and staff who support these roles. I hope you will join me in voting for them. –Amal Smith Amal Smith is a member of the Piedmont School Board. articles.text: Early Wednesday morning on October 5, a call was placed to the Piedmont Police about a parked car on fire on the 100 block of Crocker Avenue. The initial call came in at 3:29 a.m., and within five minutes the car, a Mazda CX5, was fully engulfed in flames. Members of the Police and Fire departments arrived on scene, and fire fighters extinguished the flames before it could spread. The car was thoroughly charred and was eventually towed away. Police enacted a neighborhood canvassing effort which resulted in finding some video evidence leading to a suspect vehicle. The license plate of the arson suspect was entered into the automatic license plate reader (ALPR) system. Four days later, on Sunday October 9, the suspect vehicle entered the city around 11:00 a.m. and recorded a hit on an ALPR camera at Grand and Rose Avenues. The suspect parked his car in the Safeway parking lot and walked inside. When the suspect exited the store and returned to the vehicle he was detained and arrested without incident. Piedmont Police Detective George Tucker interviewed the suspect who confessed to committing the arson by using lighter fluid and a match. The suspect had a previous association with the victim and the suspect admitted to the targeting attack resulting from prior disagreements. The suspect is identified as Tyler Gadbois, formerly of Piedmont and now a resident of Healdsburg. Gadbois was arrested for Aggravated Arson and was sent to Santa Rita jail.
